text:
Droit
de la famille — 241773

2024 QCCS 4401

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

BEAUHARNOIS

N° :

760-04-016260-243

DATE :

November 22, 2024

______________________________________________________________________

BY

THE
HONOURABLE

MARIE-HÉLÈNE DUBÉ, j.S.c.

______________________________________________________________________

W. G.

PLAINTIFF

v.

D. GR.
, ès qualitès, liquidator of the Estate of the Late J. H.

SUCCESSION
OF THE LATE J. H.

DEFENDANTS

Et al.

N° :

760-04-016290-240

JU. M.

PLAINTIFF

v.

W. G.

DEFENDANT

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

The Court must decide if X, who will turn 10
years old in a few weeks, will live with her father or with Mrs. Ju. M.,
who has been taking care of her since her mother passed away, five months ago.
Mrs. M. lives in Michigan. If she is awarded custody, X will move to Michigan.

[
2
]

X wants to live with Mrs. M., in Michigan. She
categorically refuses to have any contact with her father and her brother.

[
3
]

X’s parents were involved in a very conflictual
divorce. The father faces criminal accusations related to family violence and
his initial conditions prevented him from having any contact with the three
children. For approximately 15 months prior to the mother’s demise, X lived
exclusively with her mother and had no significant contact with her father.

[
4
]

A psychosocial evaluation was conducted when the
mother was still alive, but the report was released after her death. In the
expert’s opinion, X suffers from a conflict of loyalty instigated by her late
mother. The expert recommends granting X’s custody to her father.

[
5
]

If custody is awarded to Mrs. M., she asks to be
granted the attributes of parental authority regarding school, extracurricular
activities, travels and passport and medical care.

[
6
]

Finally, the father and Mrs. M. disagree on the
financial contributions required from the father for X’s needs and expenses.

ANALYSIS

1.

Custody

1.1

Facts

[
7
]

X is a bright, creative, and resilient young
girl. She is the third child of the late J. H. and W. G.. She has a sister, Y,
who is 19 years old, and a brother Z, aged 15.

[
8
]

X’s parents had a traditional marriage. The
mother stayed at home and was the primary caretaker. The father had his own
business and was the breadwinner.

[
9
]

In 2018, Mrs. Ju. M. worked for the family,
as a cleaning lady and babysitter for X. She moved to the United States in
2019. However, her friendship with the late mother continued after her
departure. She visited the mother and the children during the 2023 summer.

[
10
]

At the end of 2021, the father decided to
separate. However, the parents continued to reside together in the family
residence most of the time, until February 2023. On two different occasions,
the children were alone with the father for a few weeks. The mother met
Mr. D. Gr. in the summer of 2022 and moved in with him in February 2023. During this period, the mother was diagnosed with cancer.

[
11
]

During their separation process, both parents
accused each other of family violence. In 2022, the mother was accused of
assault against the father. However, he decided not to testify against the
mother and the criminal accusation was withdrawn. In March 2023, the father was
charged with sexual assault with strangulation, assault and harassment against
the mother, assault against Y and Z, dangerous driving, and threats against D.
Gr. conveyed to X.
[1]

[
12
]

The father’s conditions in the criminal file
prevented him from having any contact with the three children. Therefore, since
March 2023, the three children lived exclusively with the late mother, at
Mr. Gr.’s residence.

[
13
]

In the spring of 2024, Z expressed his wish to
resume his relationship with his father. The late mother did not object, but
she refused any type of coparenting. Z went to live with his father on April 4,
2024, after the modification of the father’s criminal conditions.

[
14
]

The mother’s cancer stopped responding to
treatment in the spring of 2024 and she died on June 2, 2024.

[
15
]

In anticipation of her death, the mother asked
Mrs. M. to become X’s guardian. Mrs. M. accepted. Mrs. M. lives in Michigan,
with her husband and her youngest child, who is 15 years old. She has eight
other children, who are adults, and who live in the United States.

[
16
]

X embraced the idea of living with Mrs. M. when
her mother would no longer be there, even if that meant moving to Michigan.
[2]

[
17
]

Mrs. M. came to Canada a couple of days prior to
the death to be with the mother and with X. And she stayed in Mr. Gr.’s residence
with X when the mother passed away.

[
18
]

Y also continues to live at Mr. Gr.’s residence.

[
19
]

The parents had jointly mandated a psychologist,
Mrs. Diane Pérusse, to assess the modalities of parenting time in the
children’s best interest. The expert completed her assessment of the five
family members while the mother was alive. She refused to meet with Mrs. M. because
she considered that it was beyond the scope of her mandate. However, her
report, dated June 21, 2024, recommends the father having custody of X because
of the mother’s death.

[
20
]

On June 25, 2024, the father applied for a
safeguard order “confirming” that he has custody of Z and X. His application
was directed against Mr. Gr..

[
21
]

On July 23, 2024, Mrs. M. petitioned the Court
for custody of X. On August 1
st
and 15
th
, she was awarded
interim custody of the child. However, X had to continue residing in Quebec
until the trial, which was fixed on October 23, 2024.

[
22
]

X spent six weeks in Michigan, in September and
October 2024, where she attended school, unbeknownst to her father. When he
discovered the child was in Michigan, he applied for a
habeas corpus

order. Mrs. M. returned with the child to Canada, on October 12, 2024, as she
had initially planned to do.

[
23
]

Before the trial, X reiterated to her lawyer
that she wants to live with Mrs. M. and that she refuses any contact with her
father.

[
24
]

After the trial, the Court rendered a safeguard
order to provide therapy to the child addressing the break-up of the
father-daughter relationship. On November 20, 2024, the lawyers informed the
Court of a failed attempt to start therapy.
[3]

[
25
]

The safeguard order also constrains X and Mrs. M.
to stay at Mr. Gr.’s residence until the present judgment is rendered. X
continues her schooling online while she is in Quebec.

[
26
]

The father’s conditions with respect to X have
been modified. At present, the father cannot be at the places where X lives and
studies and he cannot be in her presence or communicate with her, except in
accordance with a decision of the Superior Court, family division.
[4]
The father’s criminal trial is fixed for three days, starting on
May 5, 2025.

1.2

Legal Principles

[
27
]

The Supreme Court established the legal
framework to decide a custody dispute between a third party and a parent in
C.(G.) v
. V.‑F.(T.)
[5]
. The principles can be summarized as follows:

27.1.

The child’s interest is the determining factor,
as for any other decisions pertaining to the child.

27.2.

To obtain a custody award, a third party must do
the following:

1)

Rebut the presumption of favouring the parent as the better person
to provide care and affection to his own child
;

2)

Establish that the
development of the child is likely to be compromised if she is entrusted to the
parent’s care;

3)

Establish that she is able
to provide care and affection to the child, unlike the parent;

27.3.

The parent losing custody is not deprived of his
parental authority.

[
28
]

The aspects to be considered in the assessment
of the child’s interest include
[6]
:

-

The moral, intellectual, emotional and physical
needs of the child;

-

The child’s age, health and personality;

-

The child’s family environment, including the
presence of family violence, which includes spousal violence, or sexual
violence;

-

Other aspects of the child’s situation.

[
29
]

Between the ages of 8 and 11 years old, the
child’s wishes are an important element to consider without being determinant,
and they can be discarded when they do not correspond to the child’s best
interest.
[7]
When the child’s wishes are influenced by a conflict of loyalty,
they do not carry the same weight.
[8]

1.3

Discussion

1.3.1

Is the presumption in favour of the father
rebutted?

[
30
]

X’s refusal to have any contact with her father
does not necessarily mean that the father lacks parental capacity. However, it
suffices to rebut the presumption that he is the better suited person to
provide the care and affection that she needs. In
C.(G.) v
. V.‑F.(T.)
, the children’s refusal to live
with their father paved the way to an award of custody to a third party, in the
absence of wrongdoing by the surviving parent.

[
31
]

In addition, in the present case, the children’s
allegations and the pending criminal accusations relating to family violence
raise concerns about the father’s parental capacity.

[
32
]

Finally, the conditions imposed on the father in
the criminal file may have an impact on his capacity to exercise custody, even
if his parental capacity is established.

[
33
]

For all these reasons, Mrs. M. successfully
demonstrates that an inquiry into the modalities of custody corresponding to X’s
interest is necessary.

1.3.2

Is the father capable of caring for X?

[
34
]

The father’s parental capacity is questioned
because of the alleged family violence and lack of involvement in the
children’s upbringing.

[
35
]

The evidence establishes that the children have
been exposed to some family violence by the father in the past. However, this
family violence was not on the scale that the conditions banning all contacts
with the children would suggest.

[
36
]

The three children reported to the expert having
been exposed to the father’s verbal aggression during the 2021 to 2023 years. Z
denied having suffered from physical violence from his father.
[9]
X said that the father never hurt her but
that she found he was tough and mean with her mother, her sister and her
brother. She saw their father hitting Z, but without force. She also saw the
father grabbing a phone from the mother to prevent her from calling the police.
Finally, she spoke of  the threats the father would have made with respect to
Mr. Gr.. Y complained of the father banging the walls during disputes with
the mother and pushing her, on two occasions when she tried to separate her
parents during their fights.

[
37
]

When X discussed with the expert her wish not to
live with her father, she voiced her concern that fights between her brother
and her could reoccur and make her father angry, as it did, in the past.
[10]
She also said that she would see him more often if he learned to
manage his anger.
[11]
Y expressed a similar concern that the
father can lose control of his temper for menial frustrations such as a dish
placed in the sink rather than the dishwasher.
[12]

[
38
]

The expert recognizes that the father has a
tendency to be impulsive which can lead him to be aggressive when he is
frustrated. His psychological profile also reveals narcissistic traits.
However, she concluded that his parental capacity is good enough to have
custody of the children. She summarizes her analysis as
follows
[13]
:

Le père
présente des capacités parentales assez appropriées, et a historiquement
développé des relations pertinentes avec ses trois enfants ; il doit
cependant veiller à être suffisamment présent au quotidien ainsi qu’à mieux
contrôler sa colère que pendant la période de désorganisation de sa relation de
couple avec madame ;

[
39
]

The expert explains that the parents’ conflict
overwhelmed them. The three children were exposed to it. In fact, the three
children were brought into the conflict. Both parents failed at protecting the
three children from their conflict. Their anger at each other lead to
aggressive behaviours by the two parents, sometimes targeting the children.

[
40
]

The circumstances that triggered the family
violence are no longer present. The father has no anger towards the children.
He has no conflict with them. He understands their feelings. He wants to work
on the relationship with X to address her needs, her suffering, and how to be
the father that she needs. In addition, the father worked on improving his
communications skills in the context of Z’s psychosocial follow-up.

[
41
]

The father is now aware that his impulsivity can
harm the children. The odds that the father will continue to be reactive with
the children are low.

[
42
]

The father’s improved parental capacity also
appears from the care he provided to Z over the last seven months. When Z came
to live with his father, he was failing his school year, was drinking alcohol
and smoking cannabis and his ADHD and diabetes were not controlled. The father
helped him turn around his life. He made sure his son had medical care,
obtained psychosocial services from the CLSC and actively participated in them.
Since the beginning of the new school year, the child is assiduous at school
and has good results. He no longer uses alcohol or cannabis. He is in good
physical health.

[
43
]

In the Court’s opinion, X’s exposition to family
violence by her father contributed to her reluctance to see him after over a
year of interruption in their contacts, but it is not the principal cause of
it. The conflict of loyalty explained by the expert amplified her negative
feelings and negated the positive memories that would have otherwise helped X
keep things in a better perspective.

[
44
]

The expert observed the interaction between X
and her father in May 2024. She considers that their bond was better than what X’s
prior discourse indicated. She found the father to be appropriate and
respectful of X’s rhythm. X was able to display some affection to her father.
According to her, the projective tests she administered to X reveal that she
misses her father and would like to see him more, but that she worries that he
is upset at her. She points out that she saw videos of the father and X when
they lived together revealing their warm and affectionate relationship at the
time.

[
45
]

The expert’s report is replete with X’s
statements consistent with the conclusion that the mother deteriorated the
father’s image and put X in a conflict of loyalty, such as
[14]
:

45.1.

X said that the father was absent and the mother
asked him for help, which the father refused to give.

45.2.

She considers the father is more responsible of
the separation than the mother, who did not want it.

45.3.

She asked her father to get treatment but she
does not remember why since she was never afraid of him and he never hurt her.

45.4.

She said she feels more loyal to her mother than
to her father.

45.5.

The father chose his work over the family and
did not take care of her. X admitted that the mother discussed this with her
but insisted that she became aware of this independently from the mother, at a
very young age. In fact, the father was involved in the children’s activities
but the memories of the good times X had with him, seemingly vanished.

45.6.

At the beginning of the assessment, X drew her
family with her father in it. At the end of the assessment, she said that she
wanted nothing to do with him when she drew the picture.

[
46
]

X’s comments to her lawyer also support the
conclusion that she was caught in a conflict of loyalty. For example, on May
15, 2024, X said that she forgot to insist with the expert that she does not
want to live with her father, but she specifically asked the lawyer to mention
that she loves her father and does not want to hurt him.
[15]
On October
15, 2024, when X reiterated that she does not wish to live with her father, she
added that her mother also did not wish for this to happen.
[16]

[
47
]

The father is committed to provide X the
psychological help she needs to overcome the trauma she experienced in the
context of the acrimonious separation and of the loss of her mother. The
healing of his relationship with X will also require that he continues his
introspection on his contributions to her trauma.
[17]
His
testimony leads the Court to believe that he can do so.

[
48
]

Finally, the father’s availability for the
children is another area of concern. He recognized that he struggled to take
care of the three children when the mother left them with him, notably with
respect to their schoolwork. However, the situation has changed now that he
cannot rely on the mother to share the childcare responsibilities. The father
appears motivated to organize his life around his children now that he is their
only parent. As any working parent, the father will probably struggle to
balance work and family responsibilities. The determinant factor is his
willingness to face this struggle with a view of putting the children’s
interest ahead of other considerations.

[
49
]

After careful consideration of all the evidence,
the Court finds that X’s development would not be compromised if she is
entrusted to her father’s care, after therapeutic intervention to restore the
father-daughter bond.

1.3.3

Is Mrs. M. better able to care for X than the
father?

[
50
]

The expert did not assess Mrs. M.’s parental
capacity and X’s relationship with her. Her opinion that the father should have
custody is only based on him having adequate parental capacity, without
consideration for a second option. The Court cannot rely on this opinion to
decide who is better suited to care for X between the father and Mrs. M..

[
51
]

In the Court’s opinion, X needs both her father
and Mrs. M.. Entrusting her to only one of them is likely to have disastrous
impacts on X.

[
52
]

If custody is granted to the father, he
recognizes that X cannot immediately come live with him due to the severity of
the break-up in the relationship, at this point. In addition, the current
criminal conditions do not permit the father to reside at the same place as X.
Given that his conditions were modified to let him have custody of Z, the same
is likely to happen with X. However, there is no certainty and the delays are
unknown.
[18]
The father is well aware that a transition period is essential
before X can start living with him. He proposes his mother would come from
Michigan to live with X and Z, for a few months, in an AirBNB. This would
subject X to a second change of school this year, living in a temporary
apartment, and to the loss of the person who provides emotional security to
her, while there is no evidence that the paternal grandmother has a close
relationship with the child and that she would be able to respond to her
emotional needs. This suggestion would only bring more instability in the
children’s lives.

[
53
]

On the other hand, if X lives with Mrs. M., in
Michigan, on a permanent basis, she will break up all ties with her father, her
brother and her paternal side of the family.

[
54
]

For the rest of the school year, X’s best
interest commands that she remains with Mrs. M., at the condition that this period
is used to repair the relationship with the father. X must understand that her
wish to live permanently with Mrs. M. does not correspond to her best interest
and that she has to prepare herself to come back to her father, in Canada.

[
55
]

To come to this conclusion, the Court considered
the following.

[
56
]

Mrs. M. provided excellent, loving care to X
since she is with her. She is attentive to her personality, her interests, her
skills. She is very organized and leaves no loopholes in everything that needs
to be done for the child. She is committed to provide the best possible life to
X, even in the face of huge personal sacrifices. Her
husband supports her in this endeavour.

[
57
]

X trusts Mrs. M. and feels well with her and her
family. They love each other very much.

[
58
]

However, Mrs. M. does not consider Mr. G. as X’s
father, often referring to him as the “biological father.” And she does not
understand the child’s psychological need to have a healthy relationship with
him.

[
59
]

She unilaterally uprooted X from her life in
Canada and set up a new life for her, in Michigan. The Court does not doubt
that Mrs. M. had every intention to bring back X to Canada for the trial and to
respect the judgment to be rendered. However, from the perspective of the
child, she moved to Michigan on September 1, 2024
[19]
. Her
bedroom furniture is in Michigan, as well as her personal objects and family
souvenirs. She integrated a new school, in a new country, in a new language,
with emphasis on Christianity, whereas the family identified more with Judaism.
[20]
All these major changes occurred in the back of the father, while
the parties were waiting for their trial. The contempt for the father appears
even more clearly from the fact that his lawyers’ weekly emails asking for X’s
news were completely ignored.

[
60
]

Mrs. M. testified with sincerity. She does not
hide her emotions, her beliefs, and her values. There is no ambivalence in her
perception of the situation. She believes that the father is a bad man who hurt
the late mother and their children. She is completely committed to carry on the
late mother’s last wishes. For her, the mother knew what was best for X and she
will do everything in her power to ensure the maternal wishes are respected.

[
61
]

Mrs. M. is entitled to her feelings and
opinions. However, the problem is that they have become X’s feelings and
opinions. In fact, under her care, X became fearful of her father, whereas he
has done absolutely nothing during this period that could have scared the
child. Mrs. M. describes X as a child terrified by her father. She testified
about an incident  in a park when a black truck went by X and her. The child
pulled her arm to go back to the tree line because she was afraid that it was
her dad coming to get her. Mrs. M. also said that X is “
thankful to the
Crown that has protected her for the no contact order. She is afraid of
Monsieur
.”
[21]
X never conveyed that type of fear to the
expert or to her lawyer when she lived with her mother.

[
62
]

In addition, Mrs. M. has difficulty
distinguishing between herself and X. For example, she believes that she
blocked Z from calling her, at X’s request, not realizing her input in that
request. This happened because Z was insisting on retrieving his personal
effects from Mr. Gr.’s house. Mr. Gr. was away. Mrs. M. felt ill at
ease to let Z take things in the house in Mr. Gr.’s absence. Z used
improper language. Mrs. M. had reasons to stop the conversation, as she did not
have to accept disrespectful conduct from Z. However, Z’s total rejection that
followed this incident is alarming. He is a fifteen-year-old boy who had just
lost his mother. He wanted to get his personal effects but misbehaved. His
needs should not have been discarded because he was perceived as the father’s
ally instead of being seen for who he is. And X should not have been put in the
position of siding with Mrs. M. against her brother.

[
63
]

When her mother was alive, X expressed to the
expert her ambivalence about her father, despite the loyalty conflict. She was
envisaging the possibility to  go live with him in a few years. She also had a
relationship with her brother. At the time of the trial, her rejection of her
father and of her brother was total.

[
64
]

X deserves the chance to heal her relationship
with her father. She deserves the chance to have a relationship with her
brother, like she has one with her sister. The siblings should not perpetuate
the parental conflict among themselves. They need each other. The vicious
circle of the loyalty conflict due to the parents’ problems has created enough
harm. It must stop.

[
65
]

In summary, the father and Mrs. M. each have
strengths and weaknesses as potential caretakers for X.

[
66
]

Mrs. M. has more availability and experience to
provide day-to-day care to X and she is a source of emotional security for the
child who is still grieving the loss of her mother. However, her negative image
of the father and her perpetuation of the parental conflict threaten X’s future
mental and emotional equilibrium.

[
67
]

The father cannot overcome X’s refusal to be in
contact with him without therapeutic intervention. He recognizes this. But, on
the long term, living with her father will be healthier for X. The father truly
loves her, and he is committed to take care of her. He demonstrated with Z that
he can improve his parental skills. He should be able to reassure X and build
her trust with professional help. To do that, he will have to respect the fact
that there is a genuine bond between X and Mrs. M. that cannot be taken away
from X.

[
68
]

To balance X’s immediate needs and her future
well-being, the court will order shared custody of X as follows:

68.1.

From now until the end of the school year (at
the latest, June 27, 2025), X will reside with Mrs. M. who will be authorized
to bring X to Michigan. However, her custodial time and the authorization to
bring X to Michigan will be subjected to the following conditions:

1)

X and Mrs. M. will participate assiduously in a therapy with a
psychologist or a social worker duly registered at the Ordre des psychologues
du Québec or the Order of Social Workers, Family, and Marriage Therapists
of Quebec, that the father will designate and pay. In case they miss more than
one session, the father will immediately retrieve custody of the child.

2)

X will not leave the province of Quebec before having met, in
person, at least once, with the therapist in Quebec. The father will have to
ensure that the therapist is available for this meeting at the latest on
December 6,

2024.

3)

The father will have video calls with X at least once a week. The
communications will have to take place in a private room where X will be alone.

4)

During the spring school break, Mrs. M. will bring X to Quebec and X
will have to be with her father for at least two consecutive days.

5)

Mrs. M. will have to follow the instructions of the therapist on how
to restore a good image of the father and rebuild X’s trust in him.

6)

Mrs. M. will have to provide weekly reports of X’s well-being to the
father.

68.2.

At the latest on June 28, 2025, X will be
returned to Quebec, with all her belongings and furniture and will reside with
her father. However, his custodial time will be subjected to the following
conditions:

1)

Mrs. M. will have video calls with X at least once a week. The
communications will have to take place in a private room where X will be alone.

2)

If Mrs. M. travels to Quebec, X will have the right to be with her
for at least two consecutive days.

3)

Starting with the summer 2026, X will have the right to spend
one month, in Michigan, with Mrs. M..

2.

Parental authority

[
69
]

By Quebec law, as a result of the death of the
mother, the father can exercise alone the parental authority with respect to X.
[22]

[
70
]

In addition, even during Mrs. M. custodial time,
the father retains his right to supervise the maintenance and education of his
daughter.
[23]

[
71
]

There is not a shadow of evidence that it is
necessary to partially deprive the father of his parental authority, as Mrs. M.
is asking to do in her re-modified application.

[
72
]

It is also worth noting that the father is X’s
legal tutor by operation of law.
[24]
Custody
of the child does not affect her tutorship.
[25]
The
late mother’s designation of Mrs. M. as a tutor for her minor children in her
Last Will has no legal effects, as long as their father is alive and not
deprived of his parental authority.
[26]

[
73
]

The Court will authorize X to complete the
2024-2025 school year at the School A located in Michigan, for the sake of a
minimum of stability in X’s life. However, the choice of this school should not
have been made without the father. His parental authority was not respected.
Even if Mrs. M. had obtained exclusive custody of X, she would have had to
obtain the father’s consent or a court authorization to enroll X in a school.
The father has the right to communicate with the school and to obtain all
documents available to parents.

[
74
]

The father will have to provide a valid passport
for X, but he will continue to be the only person authorized to request a
passport for her. His consent will also be necessary if Mrs. M. wish to travel
with X.

[
75
]

Regarding decisions with respect to X’s extracurricular
activities, they will have to be taken jointly by Mrs. M. and the father, given
that they are closely related to the geography and the day-to-day realities.

[
76
]

As for medical decisions regarding X, only the
father will be authorized to make the non-urgent decisions. In the case of an
emergency, Mrs. M. will have to try to reach the father before making the
decision, but, if she is unable to do so, she will be authorized to provide
consent to the care required according to the medical professionals. She will
have to advise the father of the medical emergency and convey his position to
the medical professionals, if there is a disagreement between them.

[
77
]

Finally, Mrs. M. will have to advise the school
and the medical providers that the father is authorized to have a copy of all
the records concerning the child.

3.

the father’s alimentary obligation

[
78
]

Mrs. M. has no alimentary obligation with
respect to X. Even if she did not formally request a financial contribution
from the father in her application, at trial she blamed the father for not
contributing and she put into evidence the expenses that she incurred for X.

[
79
]

The father offers to pay monthly child support
of $649.17, based on the $103,000 income that Justice Duprat retained at the
interim stage, in the divorce file, on March 7, 2024. The parties made no
evidence of the father’s income.

[
80
]

The father does not agree to reimburse many of
the expenses that Mrs. M. incurred for X because she did so without his
authorization. The Court agrees that Mrs. M. should have waited for the
decision on custody prior to incurring costs for X’s relocation. However, the
father will have to pay for tuition costs limited to $6,000. First, X was in
private school in Quebec, and the father testified that this is the school
where she should have continued her education. So, the father would have had to
pay tuition costs. Second, X’s best interest requires her to finish her school
year without a change of school.

[
81
]

The father will also have to pay for the medical
and dental costs, including insurance, from December 7, 2024 to June 27, 2025.

4.

CONCLUSIONS

[
82
]

Mrs. Ju. M. and the father have in common a
sincere love for X. They must put behind their mutual disrespect for the sake
of X’s well-being because she needs both.

[
83
]

X must know that her voice has been heard even
if the outcome is not what she wishes now. The Court is convinced that her best
interest requires her to work with Mrs. M., her father and her therapist to
find peace and happiness.
